title: An online survey investigating the experiences of tic-related pain and use of pain management techniques in people with tics and tic disorders
study_type: Cross-sectional, self-selected English-language online survey with descriptive quantitative summaries and inductive thematic analysis.
population: 181 respondents aged 16–71 from 18 countries; eligibility required current tics AND tic-related pain, age≥16, suspected or confirmed tic disorder, and English literacy. Online patient/support/research channels. No adult-only or severe-persistent-adult estimate.
recruitment: Four of eight approached national TS charities advertised; an online TS community, NIHR MindTech social media and circulation to 47 TS support associations. Exposure, starts, exclusions, dropouts, response rate not given.
comparator: No randomized or population control. Separately reported tic- and pain-interference domain means, with matched contributing sets unverified.
exposure: Current self-attributed tic-related pain selected at entry; self-reported pain causes, care and management histories; no assigned intervention.

outcomes.interference: Adapted 13-domain BPI-SF-related scale scored 1–5, previous-week recall, N/A choice; each domain mean/SD reported separately for tics and pain.
outcomes.validation: No validation of expanded adaptation, full question stems, middle labels or clinically important threshold supplied in checked report.
outcomes.tic_severity: Adult Tic Questionnaire total 0–216; paper describes current severity without a separate explicit recall-window specification.
outcomes.resilience: Brief Resilience Scale; not a pain measure.
outcomes.care: Help-seeking, techniques used and perceived impact of tic treatment; bounded recall period not specified.
outcomes.qualitative: Thematic interpretations, not numerical prevalence or validated causal pathways.

numeric_results.reported_mean_gaps: All 13 tic means exceed corresponding pain means; minimum 0.05, maximum 1.12. Signs robust to conservative ordinary-rounding envelopes. Not established paired differences or adult estimates.
numeric_results.help_conflict: 71+46=117 table seekers versus 118 prose;64.6% matches 117/181, while 118/181 rounds 65.2%.71/117 rounds 60.7%;71/118 rounds 60.2%, neither prose 60.1%.No corrected count adopted.
additional_scope_relevant_conflicts: Highest tic mean 3.86 social situations omitted from prose highest-domain list
Sleep tic SD 1.31 table versus 1.21 prose
General doctor/physiotherapy counts 60/42 table versus 61/43 prose

uncertainty: SDs supplied; no relevant confidence intervals, paired covariance, item valid counts or age-stratified summaries. Rounding envelopes are numerical reporting checks, not sampling uncertainty.
negative_findings: Qualitative reports include variable tolerability and mixed perceived usefulness; no uniform benefit
Unchanged or worse pain reported with tic treatment; not causal treatment harms/effects
Authors did not measure quantitative satisfaction/appraisal of professional pain help
No prospective chronology establishing proposed tic–pain feedback cycle
followup: None prospective; one survey time point with recalled experiences.
attrition: Authors assert no missing outcomes, but N/A was permitted and handling/item counts not supplied. Recruitment/dropout flow unavailable.
adverse_events: No systematic comparative safety analysis; subjective treatment-impact reports are not incidence or causal estimates. Singleton treatment cells not republished.
risk_of_bias: Pain-selected self-selection through online support channels
Unknown item-specific N/A handling and response denominators
Cross-sectional recall; unassigned heterogeneous treatment histories
Single lead qualitative coder with discussion/refinement by second author; no causal identification
conflicts_funding: NIHR MindTech Medtech Cooperative and NIHR Nottingham Biomedical Research Centre cofunding; authors declare no relevant commercial/financial relationships.
applicability: Describes pain-related burden within a pain-experiencing mixed-age convenience sample. Cannot establish population pain prevalence, age≥18 interference estimates, or severe-persistent-adult outcomes.
cohort_overlap_status: No overlap with Małek established; distinct setting/time and no pooling. Independent replication not claimed.
claim_supported: Past-week interference was directly assessed separately from tic severity, and pain burden/support concerns deserve distinct measurement. Marginal mean and qualitative individual-priority statements are different estimands.
claim_not_supported: Representative prevalence, chronic pain duration, adult-only effects, paired significance, clinical meaningfulness, causal feedback, treatment efficacy/inefficacy, comparative self-management benefit, durable benefit, disease modification or cure.
retrieval_status: Publisher HTML/PDF and official EuropePMC XML inspected; PDF pages 5–7 visually verified. No public blank questionnaire, adult-only supplement or linked dataset located. EuropePMC flags hasSuppl=N, hasData=N. PubMed/PMC direct HTML browser-check limits.
reviewer: Research assistant, independent source-method review, separate source/arithmetic review; not clinical peer review.
correction_retraction_check: No linked correction/retraction found in publisher,official XML,Crossref or focused DOI searches; bounded finding only.
next_verification_task: Close Taylor audit absent public correction or methodological clarification. Adult descriptives require age ≥18 item valid/N/A counts, handling, means and dispersion; paired comparison additionally matched n and covariance/difference dispersion. Next distinct candidate: Marras et al. 2001 botulinum-toxin randomized crossover trial, PMID 11245710, DOI 10.1212/WNL.56.5.605. Verify whether pain-specific benefit/interference was measured separately from tic outcomes and procedure discomfort; check adult applicability, carryover and missing numerical prerequisites. Stop without pain-effect inference if no compatible endpoint or lawful full methods.
privacy: Original paraphrases and public aggregates only; no individual narratives, quotations, singleton treatment/demographic cells, family data or full-paper copies. No outreach or participant access.
